summary: Sodium fusidate is the sodium salt of fusidic acid, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic of the fusidane class active mainly against staphylococci, including many methicillin-resistant strains. It is used for staphylococcal skin and soft-tissue infections, osteomyelitis, and other staphylococcal infections, and topically for skin and eye infections. Because resistance emerges readily on monotherapy, systemic use is often combined with another anti-staphylococcal agent; hepatotoxicity (jaundice) and a major interaction with statins are key concerns.

moa: Sodium fusidate inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. It binds elongation factor G (EF-G) on the ribosome and prevents the translocation step of peptide chain elongation, blocking the cycling of EF-G. This is bacteriostatic (bactericidal at higher concentrations) and is mainly active against Gram-positive cocci, especially Staphylococcus aureus including many MRSA strains.

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy; systemic sodium fusidate should be used only if clearly necessary and after weighing benefit against risk. Topical use carries minimal systemic exposure.
lact: Small amounts may pass into breast milk; systemic use during breastfeeding should be undertaken with caution. Topical therapy, kept away from the nipple, results in negligible infant exposure.
renal: No major dose adjustment is generally required, since elimination is predominantly biliary rather than renal.
hepatic: Fusidic acid is eliminated mainly via the liver and bile and can cause reversible jaundice and hepatic dysfunction, particularly with high-dose or IV therapy. Use with caution and monitor liver function; avoid in significant hepatic or biliary disease.

major: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors / statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin, etc.) - markedly increased risk of rhabdomyolysis; combination is contraindicated/avoided
Other potentially hepatotoxic drugs (additive liver toxicity)
moderate: Ritonavir and other CYP3A/protein-bound drugs (altered levels)
Anticoagulants - monitor due to protein-binding displacement / hepatic effects
minor: Bilirubin (displacement from albumin - relevant in neonates)

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue as normal - do not double up. Keep evenly spaced doses to maintain antibiotic levels.
overdose: Overdose data are limited; expected effects are exaggerated gastrointestinal upset and hepatic disturbance. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with monitoring of liver function; because of high protein binding, dialysis is not expected to be helpful.
